---
title: "Why you tip more when the screen asks"
description: "The card machine turns to face you with three buttons and a queue behind you. Twenty percent suddenly seems reasonable. Nothing about the coffee changed."
image: /assets/social/why-you-tip-more-when-the-screen-asks-og.png
author: "Mesfin Genie"
date: "2026-09-06"
categories: [behavioural economics, everyday]
---

You buy a coffee. The screen swivels round. Fifteen, twenty, twenty-five
percent, and a small grey link that says "no tip". The person who made the
coffee is watching. So is the person behind you.

Two years ago you would have dropped a coin in a jar or not. Now you press
twenty. The machine did that.

Three things are happening at once. The options are the default, and the
default is where most people land. The choice is public, and being seen to
choose "no tip" carries a small social cost that a coin jar never did. And
the amounts are presented as percentages, which feel smaller than the dollars
they represent. A dollar on a five-dollar coffee is a lot; twenty percent
sounds modest.

None of this is an accident. The companies that make these systems publish
figures showing how much tipping rises when the buttons appear, and the
figures are large.

I am not against tipping. I am against not noticing when a choice has been
made for me. So here is the small act of independence: decide what you tip
for a coffee before you reach the counter. Then, when the screen turns, you
are not deciding under pressure with three people watching. You are just
confirming.

It sounds trivial. It is also exactly the skill that keeps you from being
steered in rooms where the stakes are higher.
